name: Idiopathic Anaphylaxis

prevalence.estimate: Estimated 20,000-50,000 cases in the United States
prevalence.range: Annual incidence of anaphylaxis is 50-112 per 100,000; idiopathic accounts for ~20-30% of anaphylaxis cases

criteria.description: Fulfills clinical criteria for anaphylaxis (acute onset involving skin/mucosal tissue AND respiratory compromise and/or hypotension, OR involvement of two or more organ systems after exposure to likely allergen)
No identifiable trigger despite thorough evaluation including allergy testing, food diary, and medication review
Exclusion of clonal mast cell disorder (normal baseline tryptase, negative KIT D816V, normal bone marrow if indicated)
Acute serum tryptase elevated during episode (>11.4 ng/mL or >20% + 2 ng/mL above baseline)
Recurrent episodes (frequent = >=6 episodes per year or >=2 in 2 months; infrequent = fewer)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Clinical anaphylaxis without identifiable trigger after thorough allergic evaluation and exclusion of mast cell clonal disease
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Classified as frequent (>=6/year or >=2 within 2 months) or infrequent. Many initially diagnosed as idiopathic are later reclassified when a trigger is found. Must also exclude hereditary angioedema, carcinoid, pheochromocytoma, and other mimics.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Recurrent episodes meeting anaphylaxis criteria without identifiable trigger
pathognomonic.notes: Defining feature: anaphylaxis of unknown cause
searchTerms: repeated severe allergic reactions without known cause

occasional.symptomName: Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea
searchTerms: stomach pain with nausea and vomiting
seizures caused by low brain blood flow
fits due to reduced brain circulation

laboratory: Acute serum tryptase elevated during episode (draw within 15 min to 3 hours of onset)
Baseline serum tryptase normal (distinguishes from mastocytosis)
24-hour urine histamine metabolites may be elevated during episodes
Negative specific IgE testing to common allergens
Normal C4 and C1-inhibitor levels (excludes hereditary angioedema)
imaging: CT chest/abdomen if carcinoid or other tumor suspected
genetic: Consider TPSAB1 copy number testing (hereditary alpha-tryptasemia may predispose)
other: Comprehensive allergy evaluation: skin prick testing, specific IgE panels, food challenge if indicated
Bone marrow biopsy if baseline tryptase elevated or frequent severe episodes (exclude mastocytosis)
Drug provocation testing if medication trigger suspected

distinguishingFeatures: MCAS has chronic episodic multisystem symptoms, not just acute anaphylaxis
Idiopathic anaphylaxis is defined by discrete anaphylactic episodes
SM has elevated baseline tryptase, KIT D816V, and bone marrow abnormalities
Idiopathic anaphylaxis has normal baseline tryptase and bone marrow
HAE has low C4 and low C1-inhibitor (Type I) or dysfunctional C1-inhibitor (Type II)
HAE does not typically cause urticaria or hypotension
Food allergy has identifiable trigger on skin prick/specific IgE testing
Idiopathic anaphylaxis occurs without identifiable food trigger

redFlags: Episodes with cardiovascular collapse or cardiac arrest
Progressive increase in episode severity or frequency
references: Greenberger PA, et al. Idiopathic anaphylaxis. Immunol Allergy Clin North Am. 2015;35(2):349-362.
Ditto AM, et al. Idiopathic anaphylaxis: a series of 335 cases. Ann Allergy Asthma Immunol. 1996;77(4):285-291.
Akin C. Mast cell activation syndromes. J Allergy Clin Immunol. 2017;140(2):349-355.
